candidates.attacker_control: The characters being filtered come from the wrapped Reader (e.g. a file/buffer/content that a caller filters before further processing). Whoever supplies that content controls the characters that are supposed to be stripped but are instead delivered verbatim on the bulk-read path. The caller only chooses the skip characters and reads via the public Reader API.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked the single-character read() override (correct, so the bypass is specific to the bulk-read path); checked the compaction bounds (pos < readPos) so the defect is confined to filter/count semantics, not a buffer overrun; checked both subclasses' filter() implementations to confirm the argument semantics (a character, not a count); checked that the classes are public and reachable from ordinary callers; verified via repository search that this is the only occurrence of a predicate being passed a read count in this style (search for "(read)" matches only line 64), which argues against it being a deliberate design.
candidates.impact: Sanitization/validation bypass: characters the caller asked to be removed (control characters, quotes, separators, CR/LF or any configured junk characters) are delivered unfiltered whenever the data is read in blocks, which is the usual path (BufferedReader, IOUtils/FileUtils). If the filter is used as a security control before writing CSV, logs or passing data to another component, it is ineffective on that path, enabling downstream injection or parsing/corruption issues; conversely, blocks whose length equals a skip code point are silently dropped, causing unexpected data loss. There is no memory-safety impact (the pos < readPos guard keeps writes in bounds).
candidates.prerequisites: A consumer uses CharacterFilterReader/CharacterSetFilterReader (or a subclass) as a sanitization step and consumes the data through read(char[]), read(char[],int,int), BufferedReader.readLine/fill, IOUtils.copy(Reader,...), FileUtils.readLines/readFileToString or any other bulk-read based path, and relies on the removed characters being gone. Consumers that only call the single-character read() are unaffected. No special JVM, privilege or configuration conditions are needed; the classes are public API in a widely used library.
candidates.root_cause: In AbstractCharacterFilterReader.read(char[] cbuf, int off, int len) the compaction loop tests `filter(read)`, i.e. it passes the number of characters returned by the delegate read instead of the character at the current position (`filter(cbuf[readPos])`). Because `read` is constant for the whole call, the outcome no longer depends on the data: when `read` is not one of the configured skip code points (the normal case) no character is ever filtered and every skip character survives into the caller's buffer; when `read` happens to equal a skip code point, the entire just-read block is silently discarded and the method returns 0. The single-character read() override (lines 39-44) correctly tests `filter(ch)`, so the class behaves correctly or not depending on which read API the consumer uses. Subclasses CharacterFilterReader and CharacterSetFilterReader inherit the broken override.
candidates.title: Character filter readers bypass character filtering on the bulk read(char[], int, int) path
candidates.trace: Consumer calls read(cbuf, off, len) (line 57) -> super.read(...) fills the buffer and returns `read` (line 58) -> loop iterates readPos = off .. off+read-1 (line 63) -> predicate evaluated as filter(read) (line 64), always the same boolean for the block -> if false, `continue` is never taken, pos advances in lock-step with readPos (line 67-70 does not compact anything), and the method returns `read`, so all characters including configured skip characters remain in cbuf; if true, `continue` is taken for every position, pos stays off-1, and the method returns 0 while the underlying data has already been consumed (silent data loss). The intended per-character check is visible in read() (line 43: while (filter(ch))) and in the subclasses' filter implementations (CharacterFilterReader line 45 compares ch to the configured skip character; CharacterSetFilterReader line 52 looks the character up in the skip set), confirming that the argument to filter() must be a character, not a count.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed: no tests or code were executed, and no test sources are exposed in this snapshot. The defect itself is derived directly from the source; the severity depends on whether a particular consumer treats the filter as a security control. I could not compare this file against upstream history, so I cannot say whether the line is a historical upstream bug or a deliberately introduced mutation; either way the current source behavior is as described.
candidates.weakness_type: Protection mechanism failure / improper input validation (sanitization filter bypass) — CWE-693/CWE-20

coverage_summary: All 168 files reported by get_source_scope were accounted for: root build/config/docs files plus src/main/java sources and src/site xdoc files (no src/test files are exposed by the scope filter). I read the security-relevant input/output stream readers and wrappers, the filefilter package family, the serialization package, the core FilenameUtils/FileUtils/FileDeleteStrategy/FileCleaningTracker/LockableFileWriter/FileSystemUtils classes, and the monitor/DirectoryWalker classes, and ran targeted searches for exec/Runtime, reflection/forName, MessageDigest, URL handling, canonical/exists/startsWith checks, null-byte validation, and wrong-argument predicate patterns. The strongest, most localizable defect found is the AbstractCharacterFilterReader bulk-read filter bypass described in the candidate; other areas examined matched expected behavior (bounds checks, null-byte checks, exec via fixed argument arrays, delete/symlink handling).
limitations: No test sources, build execution, dependency resolution or runtime verification were available; all conclusions are static source readings.
No upstream/diff baseline is available, so I cannot distinguish a deliberately introduced mutation from a historical upstream defect in AbstractCharacterFilterReader.

Large files (FileUtils, IOUtils, FilenameUtils, XmlStreamReader, Tailer, ReversedLinesFileReader, WriterOutputStream, ReaderInputStream) were reviewed selectively rather than line-by-line; additional defects cannot be excluded.
The one-candidate cap means only the single strongest lead is reported; the normalize() path-traversal behavior is real in this version but was not submitted.
Severity of the selected candidate depends on how downstream applications use the filter readers (security control vs. cosmetic cleanup).

rejected_leads.lead: FilenameUtils.normalize/getPrefixLength limited path traversal (input such as "//../foo" is returned unchanged because getPrefixLength treats the leading "//.." segment as a UNC server/share prefix; known upstream issue CVE-2021-29425 affecting this version).
rejected_leads.reason: Real but limited: the advisory impact is a one-level traversal and only materialises if a caller uses normalize() as a security boundary when building filesystem paths; the code is long-standing across releases rather than a localizable anomaly, so it is weaker than the filter bypass as a single candidate for this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: XmlStreamReader.getXmlProlog (lines 701-746) loops on is.read(...) and does not detect a delegate stream that repeatedly returns 0 for a positive-length read, allowing a CPU spin (later addressed upstream as CVE-2024-47554).
rejected_leads.reason: Requires a non-conforming/pathological InputStream and yields at most a DoS; the loop is otherwise bounded to a 4096-byte buffer, so the source evidence for a concrete exploitable impact is weaker than the selected candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: ValidatingObjectInputStream (serialization package) overrides resolveClass but not resolveProxyClass, so proxy class names are not validated against the accept/reject matchers.
rejected_leads.reason: Design limitation of the whitelist mechanism rather than a demonstrated bypass in this snapshot; exploitability depends on the consumer's proxy usage and is not verifiable from the source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: FileSystem.isReservedFileName uses Arrays.binarySearch against a case-sensitive reserved-name list (WINDOWS enum), potentially allowing reserved names with different casing.
rejected_leads.reason: Functional/compatibility gap with no clear attacker-controlled confidentiality or integrity impact in this library context, and the list/lookup semantics are otherwise consistent.

summary: Scope: the 168-file Apache Commons IO snapshot (2.7-SNAPSHOT, mid-2018 state per changes.xml ending at IO-577), main Java sources plus site/build files; no test sources are exposed. I reviewed the stream/reader composites, file filters, serialization package, and the core FilenameUtils/FileUtils/FileSystemUtils path, copy, delete and process logic, and searched for dangerous sinks (exec, deserialization/reflection, XML parsing, URL handling, crypto, path normalization). The single strongest source-evidenced defect is in the newly added character-filter readers (IO-577): the bulk-read override in AbstractCharacterFilterReader applies the per-character filter predicate to the number of characters read instead of to each character, so the filtering control is effectively disabled (or over-applied) on the standard read(char[]/int,int) path. I selected that as the one candidate; a genuine but limited upstream path-normalization issue in FilenameUtils and a pathological-stream read loop in XmlStreamReader were evaluated and left as rejected leads.
